---
title: "Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure"
---

A crystal structure is often first encountered as a picture: coloured spheres,
polyhedra, chains, layers or frameworks. The picture is useful, but it is not
the structure itself. A crystallographic model is a compact mathematical
description of a periodic arrangement. In this laboratory we will start from
that description and reconstruct the structure step by step.

The practical question is simple:

> **How does the information stored in a CIF become the periodic crystal that
> we draw and interpret?**

This is the first computational activity because it establishes a workflow that
will return throughout the course: a structural model is read from data,
analysed, visualized, checked against symmetry, and eventually used as the
starting point for calculations of energy and physical properties.

## The CIF as a crystallographic description

The **Crystallographic Information File (CIF)** is a structured text format.
For the present exercise, the most important information is the unit cell, the
space group, the atomic sites, their fractional coordinates and their
occupancies.

The fractional coordinate $(x,y,z)$ does not give a distance in ångström.
Instead, it gives a position relative to the three direct-lattice vectors
$\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$:

$$
\mathbf{r} = x\mathbf{a} + y\mathbf{b} + z\mathbf{c}.
$$

This is why the same fractional coordinates can describe geometrically
different Cartesian positions when the cell parameters change.

A CIF normally does not need to list every atom that appears in a conventional
unit cell. It can store only the crystallographically independent sites. The
remaining sites follow from the symmetry of the space group.

## Asymmetric unit and unit cell

The **asymmetric unit** is the smallest part of the structure from which the
contents of the unit cell can be generated by applying the appropriate
space-group operations. The **unit cell**, in turn, generates the infinite
periodic crystal by translation.

This distinction is easy to lose when looking only at a structure drawing.
MgO provides a particularly clean example. Only one Mg site and one O site are
needed in its crystallographic description, but applying the symmetry and
centring operations generates the complete contents of the conventional cubic
cell.

In the notebook we therefore inspect the structure twice: first as the list of
sites written in the CIF, and then as the symmetry-expanded unit cell. The
difference between these lists is itself part of the crystallographic
information.

## Two complementary symmetry tools

We use **Gemmi** and **spglib** for different reasons.

Gemmi is used to read the CIF as a crystallographic document. It understands
the unit cell, space-group symbols, symmetry operations and atomic sites. In
other words, it can tell us what crystallographic information the file claims
to contain.

spglib approaches the problem from another direction. We give it lattice
vectors, atomic coordinates and atomic species. It then searches numerically
for operations that map the structure onto itself. This requires a tolerance,
because coordinates in real structure files are finite-precision numbers and
experimental structures are never mathematical abstractions with infinitely
exact coordinates.

The comparison is useful:

$$
\text{symmetry stated in the CIF}
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{symmetry implied by the numerical structure}.
$$

Agreement is a consistency check. Disagreement is not something to hide by
changing parameters until the desired answer appears. It is a result that must
be understood: the structure may be distorted, the tolerance may be
inappropriate, the CIF may use a non-standard setting, or the structural model
may contain disorder or partial occupancies.

For this first exercise we use ordered structures with full occupancies so that
the symmetry analysis remains unambiguous.

## Symmetry operations in coordinate form

A space-group operation can be written as a transformation of fractional
coordinates. The identity is

$$
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(x,y,z),
$$

whereas an operation written, for example, as

```text
-y,x,z
```

maps

$$
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(-y,x,z).
$$

Translations may appear as fractional additions such as $1/2$. Rather than
printing every operation of a high-symmetry space group without context, the
notebook first shows a compact set of Hall-derived operations and the lattice
centring translations, and then lets you inspect part of the full operation
list.

The software can describe the matrix and translational parts of an operation,
but interpreting an operation geometrically remains a crystallographic task.
In particular, the presence of a translational component is what distinguishes
operations such as screw axes and glide planes from their purely point-symmetry
counterparts.

## Wyckoff positions

The atoms of a crystal can also be organized into **Wyckoff positions**.
A Wyckoff position identifies an orbit of symmetrically equivalent points in a
given space group.

Three pieces of information are especially useful:

- the **multiplicity**, which gives the number of equivalent sites in the
  conventional unit cell;
- the **Wyckoff letter**, which distinguishes inequivalent orbits;
- the **site symmetry**, which describes the subgroup of operations that leaves
  a particular site invariant.

A multiplicity is therefore not the number of independent atoms that had to be
entered in the CIF. Quite the opposite: several atoms in the conventional cell
may all be generated from one crystallographically independent site.

## Visualization is inspection, not proof

The notebooks use **py3Dmol** to display the CIF interactively. You can rotate
the structure, zoom, draw the unit-cell box and replicate the cell to make
periodicity easier to see.

The default representation uses spheres without automatically inferred bonds.
This choice is deliberate. A line drawn between two atoms by a visualization
program is based on a graphical or distance criterion; it is not itself a
crystallographic observable and should not silently determine how we interpret
bonding in a mineral.

The viewer is therefore an aid to scientific inspection. The quantitative
description still comes from the crystallographic data and symmetry analysis.

## Laboratory workflow

The activity has two parts.

First, we work together on **MgO (periclase)**:

```text
01-guided-mgo.ipynb
```

MgO is useful because the rocksalt structure is simple enough that the
relationship between asymmetric unit, face-centred cell, symmetry and Wyckoff
multiplicity remains visible.

You will then receive a second CIF and repeat the same reasoning independently
in:

```text
02-assigned-structure.ipynb
```

Place the assigned CIF directly inside:

```text
work/lab01/
```

and change only the filename requested in the notebook.

The questions are intentionally short. They ask you to interpret the structure,
not to reproduce Python code.
